title: Nucleotide Metabolism: Build It, Recycle It, or Pay in Uric Acid

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Hypoxanthine is a purine base. What is it called once a ribose is attached, and what once a phosphate is added to that ribose?
cards.back: Inosine (a nucleoside), then IMP (a nucleotide).
cards.why: Base + ribose = nucleoside; nucleoside + phosphate on the ribose = nucleotide.
cards.quote: Add a ribose and it is a nucleoside; add a phosphate to that ribose and it is a nucleotide.
cards.section: Three words first: base, nucleoside, nucleotide

cards.front: {{c1::IMP}} is the first purine nucleotide the cell builds, and the parent of both AMP and GMP.
cards.quote: IMP is the first purine nucleotide the cell builds, and the parent of both AMP and GMP.
cards.section: Three words first: base, nucleoside, nucleotide

cards.front: Picture a cell's purine nucleotides as a pool on a loop. What are the two doors in and the one way out?
cards.back: In: de novo synthesis (build) and salvage (recycle freed bases). Out: breakdown, almost all of it leaving as uric acid.
cards.quote: A cell's purine nucleotides are a pool on a loop, with two doors in (build and recycle) and one way out.
cards.section: Two doors in, one way out

cards.front: In a non-growing body at steady state, how much purine does a cell build de novo, and what does the body's uric acid output equal?
cards.back: It builds what it fails to recycle. Uric acid made equals purine built plus purine absorbed from food.
cards.why: Exceptions: growing tissue builds extra, and sudden loss of many cells sends their nucleic acids into the exit.
cards.quote: the uric acid the body makes equals what it builds plus the purine it absorbs from food.
cards.section: Two doors in, one way out

cards.front: A person eats a purine-rich meal. Does most of that food purine refill the body's nucleotide pools, or does it raise uric acid output? Why?
cards.back: It mostly raises uric acid output. Food purine is largely broken down in the gut wall and liver rather than reused, so it adds to the exit, not the pool.
cards.quote: Food purine is mostly broken down in the gut wall and liver rather than reused, so it adds to the exit, not the pool.
cards.section: Two doors in, one way out

cards.front: How is PRPP (5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate) made, and by which enzyme?
cards.back: PRPP synthetase moves a pyrophosphate from ATP onto carbon 1 of ribose-5-phosphate (from the pentose phosphate pathway), leaving AMP.
cards.quote: PRPP synthetase takes that pyrophosphate from ATP, leaving AMP.
cards.section: The molecule both doors use: PRPP

cards.front: Why is attaching a base or amino group to carbon 1 of PRPP effectively irreversible?
cards.back: The pyrophosphate leaves on attachment, and its rapid breakdown pulls the reaction forward, making it effectively one-way.
cards.quote: when something attaches to carbon 1 the pyrophosphate leaves, and its rapid breakdown makes the attachment effectively one-way.
cards.section: The molecule both doors use: PRPP

cards.front: PRPP synthesis uses one ATP molecule. Why does it count as 2 ATP equivalents?
cards.back: The ATP becomes AMP, spending two high-energy phosphate bonds; the AMP must be recharged twice to become ATP again.
cards.quote: PRPP uses one ATP molecule, but turning it into AMP spends two bonds, and the AMP must be recharged twice to become ATP again.
cards.section: The molecule both doors use: PRPP

cards.front: What are the sources of the nine atoms of the purine ring?
cards.back: Glycine (3), glutamine (2), aspartate (1), CO₂ (1), and two formyl carbons carried by tetrahydrofolate (THF).
cards.quote: The ring's nine atoms come from glycine (three), glutamine (two), aspartate (one), CO₂ (one) and two one-carbon (formyl) groups

cards.front: De novo purine synthesis: PRPP costs 2 ATP equivalents, four ring-building steps each turn ATP into ADP, and IMP to AMP uses one GTP to GDP. What does one AMP cost, and how many times more than salvaging adenine (PRPP only)?
cards.back: IMP = 2 + 4 = 6 ATP-eq; AMP = 6 + 1 = 7 ATP-eq. Salvage costs 2, so building is 7/2 = 3.5 times as costly.
cards.why: One ATP equivalent is one high-energy phosphate bond spent; GTP to GDP counts the same as ATP to ADP.
cards.quote: Costs here are counted in ATP equivalents: one high-energy phosphate bond spent, as when ATP becomes ADP (a GTP becoming GDP counts the same).
cards.section: The molecule both doors use: PRPP

cards.front: IMP costs 6 ATP equivalents to build, and IMP to GMP spends one ATP to AMP. Salvage of guanine by HGPRT costs only the PRPP. Compare the costs of GMP by the two routes.
cards.back: De novo GMP = 6 + 2 = 8 ATP-eq. Salvage = 2 ATP-eq (the PRPP). Building costs 8/2 = 4 times as much.
cards.why: ATP to AMP spends two bonds; salvage needs no amino acids or folate.
cards.quote: The only cost is the PRPP, 2 ATP equivalents, with no amino acids or folate: three to four times cheaper than building.

cards.front: Which purine salvage enzyme handles which bases, and what does each make?
cards.back: HGPRT: hypoxanthine to IMP and guanine to GMP. APRT: adenine to AMP. Both move phosphoribose from PRPP onto the base in one step.
cards.quote: HGPRT (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase) turns hypoxanthine into IMP and guanine into GMP; APRT (adenine phosphoribosyltransferase) turns adenine into AMP.

cards.front: What is the committed step of de novo purine synthesis, and what does the enzyme do?
cards.back: Glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase: it swaps PRPP's pyrophosphate for an amino group from glutamine, the first step that sends PRPP to purines only.
cards.why: Before this step PRPP can still go to salvage, pyrimidines or NAD⁺, so this is the place for control.
cards.quote: The first step that sends it to purines only is glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase, which swaps PRPP's pyrophosphate for an amino group from glutamine.
cards.section: The gate: where the cell decides to build

cards.front: How is glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase switched on and off?
cards.back: On: PRPP, its substrate, also activates it. Off: IMP, AMP and GMP bind away from the active site (feedback inhibition); AMP plus GMP together inhibit more than either alone.
cards.quote: IMP, AMP and GMP bind the enzyme away from its active site and switch it off (feedback inhibition).
cards.section: The gate: where the cell decides to build

cards.front: A cell with plenty of AMP and GMP is given free hypoxanthine. Predict its rate of de novo purine synthesis and give two reasons.
cards.back: It falls. Salvaging the hypoxanthine spends PRPP, leaving the gate less substrate and activator, and it makes IMP, which adds to feedback inhibition.
cards.why: Recycling saves ATP and also turns building down.
cards.quote: Recycling does more than save ATP: it turns building down.
cards.section: The gate: where the cell decides to build

cards.front: Which enzyme makes uric acid in human purine breakdown, and from what?
cards.back: Xanthine oxidase, in two oxidations: hypoxanthine to xanthine, then xanthine to uric acid.
cards.quote: Oxidize twice: xanthine oxidase turns hypoxanthine into xanthine, and xanthine into uric acid.

cards.front: How do adenine nucleotides and guanine reach the xanthine oxidase steps of purine breakdown?
cards.back: AMP and adenosine lose adenine's amino group to become inosine; removing the ribose gives hypoxanthine. Guanine loses its amino group and joins at xanthine.
cards.quote: Guanine joins at xanthine, by losing its amino group.

cards.front: Why do humans, unlike most mammals, end purine breakdown at uric acid, and why does that matter?
cards.back: Humans and other apes lost a working uricase, which in most mammals starts converting uric acid to highly soluble allantoin. Sparingly soluble uric acid is our end product, so we are prone to gout.
cards.quote: Humans and the other apes lost a working uricase during evolution, so for us sparingly soluble uric acid is the end product.

cards.front: Two adults both lack uricase, as all humans do. One develops gout and the other never does. What mostly explains the difference?
cards.back: How well each person's kidneys and gut excrete urate. Missing uricase makes humans prone to gout, but excretion mostly decides who gets it.
cards.quote: That missing enzyme is why humans are prone to gout, though who gets it depends mostly on how well the kidneys and gut excrete urate.

cards.front: Above roughly what serum urate concentration is urate supersaturated, and what does it form?
cards.back: About 6.8 mg/dL. It can slowly crystallize as monosodium urate in and around joints; a gout flare is inflammation against those crystals.
cards.quote: Once serum urate (uric acid's ionized form, the one in blood) climbs past roughly 6.8 mg/dL, it is supersaturated

cards.front: How does allopurinol lower urate in gout?
cards.back: It is a hypoxanthine look-alike that inhibits xanthine oxidase, so less urate is made; over months the crystals can dissolve.
cards.why: Other gout drugs work differently, by helping the kidneys excrete more urate.
cards.quote: Allopurinol, a hypoxanthine look-alike, inhibits xanthine oxidase, so urate production falls and, over months, the crystals can dissolve.

cards.front: In Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, which enzyme is missing, and why are nearly all patients boys?
cards.back: HGPRT, the purine salvage enzyme. Its gene is on the X chromosome.
cards.quote: In Lesch-Nyhan syndrome the HGPRT gene, on the X chromosome, does not work, so nearly all patients are boys.

cards.front: A cell has no HGPRT. Trace what happens to freed hypoxanthine and guanine, to PRPP, to the purine-synthesis gate, and to uric acid.
cards.back: The bases cannot be salvaged, so they are oxidized to uric acid. Unspent PRPP piles up and pushes the gate open, so building speeds up, and that extra purine also leaves as uric acid.
cards.why: The cell builds what it fails to recycle, and now it fails to recycle far more.
cards.quote: The PRPP that salvage would have spent piles up and pushes the gate open, so building speeds up.

cards.front: A boy with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is given allopurinol. His urate falls. Will his movement problems and self-injury improve?
cards.back: No. Allopurinol protects kidneys and joints, but the neurological disease is not caused by urate, and its mechanism is not fully understood.
cards.why: Losing HGPRT does two separate kinds of harm; allopurinol treats only the urate flood.
cards.quote: Losing HGPRT does two separate kinds of harm, and allopurinol treats only the urate flood.

cards.front: What structural rule separates purine from pyrimidine synthesis?
cards.back: Purines build the ring directly on PRPP's ribose-phosphate. Pyrimidines build the ring first, from carbamoyl phosphate and aspartate, and attach ribose-phosphate from PRPP afterward.
cards.quote: they build the ring first, from carbamoyl phosphate and aspartate, and take the ribose-phosphate from PRPP only afterward.

cards.front: Contrast CPS-I (urea cycle) and CPS-II (pyrimidine synthesis) by location, nitrogen source and regulator.
cards.back: CPS-I: mitochondrial, free ammonia, needs N-acetylglutamate. CPS-II: cytosolic, glutamine's nitrogen, shut off by UTP.
cards.why: Separate places and signals let nitrogen disposal and nucleotide building run independently.
cards.quote: CPS-I is mitochondrial, takes free ammonia and needs N-acetylglutamate; CPS-II is cytosolic, takes glutamine's nitrogen and is shut off by UTP, a finished pyrimidine.

cards.front: Why does pyrimidine breakdown never cause gout?
cards.back: Pyrimidines break down to soluble products: β-alanine, β-aminoisobutyrate, CO₂ and ammonia.
cards.quote: pyrimidines break down to soluble products (β-alanine, β-aminoisobutyrate, CO₂ and ammonia), so they have no gout.

cards.front: In a dividing cell, which enzyme supplies most new dNTPs, and which drug inhibits it?
cards.back: Ribonucleotide reductase, which reduces ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides. Hydroxyurea inhibits it (used in sickle-cell disease and some leukemias).
cards.quote: In a dividing cell most new dNTPs (deoxynucleoside triphosphates) come through one gateway, ribonucleotide reductase, which reduces ribonucleotides

cards.front: Thymidylate synthase makes dTMP from dUMP. Why does continued dTMP synthesis depend on dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR)?
cards.back: Thymidylate synthase uses a folate-carried carbon and leaves the folate as DHF. DHFR must turn DHF back into THF before it can carry another carbon.
cards.quote: Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) must turn DHF back into THF before it can carry another carbon, to thymidylate or to the purine ring.

cards.front: Why do antimetabolite drugs hit dividing cancer cells hardest, and why do they cause side effects?
cards.back: Dividing cells need nucleotides fastest. Fast-dividing normal tissues share that need, so they are hit too.
cards.quote: The dividing cell is the most exposed, because it needs nucleotides fastest, though fast-dividing normal tissues are hit too.

cards.front: Methotrexate, a folate mimic, blocks DHFR. Predict which two parts of nucleotide synthesis it starves.
cards.back: THF is not regenerated, so de novo purine synthesis loses its two folate carbons, and thymidylate synthase loses the carbon that makes dTMP.
cards.quote: Methotrexate mimics folate and jams DHFR, so THF is not regenerated, starving both the purine ring's two folate carbons and the carbon that makes dTMP.

cards.front: How does 5-fluorouracil stop DNA synthesis?
cards.back: It mimics uracil and inside the cell becomes FdUMP, which traps thymidylate synthase, starving the cell of dTMP.
cards.quote: Inside the cell it becomes FdUMP, which traps thymidylate synthase itself, so it too starves the cell of the dTMP it needs to copy its DNA.

cards.front: A leukemia cell acquires a mutation that inactivates HGPRT. What happens when it meets 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP), and why?
cards.back: It is resistant. 6-MP enters through the salvage door, so without HGPRT it is never made into counterfeit nucleotides, and the cell still builds purines de novo.
cards.quote: Without HGPRT, 6-MP is never made into nucleotides, and the cell can still build its purines de novo.

cards.front: You want to isolate HGPRT-deficient mutants from a culture of cells. Design a selection using a purine analog, and explain why the survivors can still grow.
cards.back: Grow the cells in 6-thioguanine, which selects HGPRT-mutant cells. HGPRT-deficient cells survive because they still build purines de novo.
cards.why: Rests on the lesson's statement that 6-thioguanine selects HGPRT-mutant cells in culture.
cards.quote: That is why the related drug 6-thioguanine selects HGPRT-mutant cells in culture.

cards.front: A treatment will kill a large, fast-growing tumor within days. Predict serum urate. What do you give before treatment, and what if urate is already high?
cards.back: Urate surges: dying cells release nucleic acids and nucleotides, whose purines exit as uric acid (tumor lysis) and can crystallize in the kidneys. Give allopurinol beforehand to block xanthine oxidase; urate already present needs rasburicase.
cards.why: Allopurinol only stops new urate being made; rasburicase is a drug form of uricase that breaks existing urate down.
cards.quote: Allopurinol given beforehand blocks the exit's last two steps, so less urate is made.

cards.front: Acyclovir is a guanosine look-alike. What does it target, and how does that differ from the other nucleotide drugs?
cards.back: It jams the herpes virus's own DNA polymerase, rather than the host's nucleotide doors, exit or DNA branch.
cards.quote: acyclovir, a guanosine look-alike, instead jams the herpes virus's own DNA polymerase.

cards.front: Which enzyme on the way from IMP to GMP uses NAD⁺, and which transplant drug targets it?
cards.back: IMP dehydrogenase; mycophenolate.
cards.quote: IMP dehydrogenase, on the way to GMP, uses an NAD⁺ and is the target of the transplant drug mycophenolate.
cards.section: The fine print of the tally

cards.front: From IMP, making AMP requires GTP and making GMP requires ATP. What does this cross-requirement accomplish for the two pools?
cards.back: It helps balance the adenine and guanine nucleotide pools.
cards.why: Rests on the stated rule that AMP needs GTP and GMP needs ATP.
cards.quote: That AMP needs GTP and GMP needs ATP helps balance the two pools.
cards.section: The fine print of the tally

cards.front: A patient has normal HGPRT but an overactive PRPP synthetase. Predict urate and gout risk, using the purine gate.
cards.back: Urate overproduction and gout. Extra PRPP pushes the glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase gate open, so building rises, and the excess purine leaves as uric acid.
cards.why: Same logic as Lesch-Nyhan: PRPP is both the gate's substrate and its activator.
cards.quote: An overactive PRPP synthetase pushes the gate open even with working HGPRT: urate overproduction and gout by the same logic.

cards.front: Allopurinol is given to a gout patient with working HGPRT and to a boy with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. Contrast what happens to total purine output in each.
cards.back: With HGPRT, the hypoxanthine left behind is salvaged, so allopurinol tends to lower total purine output, not just urate. In Lesch-Nyhan it only swaps urate for hypoxanthine and xanthine, risking xanthine stones.
cards.why: Salvage spends PRPP and adds feedback, turning building down; without HGPRT that brake is absent.
cards.quote: With working HGPRT, allopurinol tends to lower total purine output, not just urate, because the hypoxanthine it leaves behind is salvaged.

cards.front: An infant has an inherited block in pyrimidine synthesis at the step just after orotate. What compound appears in the urine?
cards.back: Orotate, which accumulates and spills into the urine (orotic aciduria).
cards.quote: In orotic aciduria, an inherited block after orotate, orotate spills into the urine.

cards.front: How does mammalian ribonucleotide reductase keep the four dNTPs balanced?
cards.back: One allosteric site sets overall activity; another sets which ribonucleoside diphosphate it reduces. Mis-tuning is mutagenic.
cards.quote: one allosteric site sets its overall activity and another sets which substrate it reduces, keeping the four dNTPs balanced (mis-tuning is mutagenic).

cards.front: Leucovorin, a ready-made reduced folate, is given with methotrexate and also with 5-fluorouracil. Explain why it weakens one drug and strengthens the other.
cards.back: With methotrexate it bypasses the blocked DHFR, so normal cells get reduced folate and are rescued. With 5-FU it supplies the folate partner that locks FdUMP onto thymidylate synthase.
cards.quote: Leucovorin, a ready-made reduced folate, bypasses DHFR and rescues normal cells from methotrexate.

cards.front: A leukemia patient on 6-mercaptopurine is started on allopurinol. Why must the 6-MP dose be cut?
cards.back: Xanthine oxidase also breaks down 6-MP. Blocking it with allopurinol raises 6-MP levels, so the same dose becomes too much.
cards.quote: Xanthine oxidase also breaks 6-MP down, so giving allopurinol with 6-MP means cutting the 6-MP dose.

cards.front: A patient with low TPMT (thiopurine methyltransferase) activity receives a standard 6-MP dose. Predict the outcome.
cards.back: Toxicity. TPMT inactivates 6-MP, so with low TPMT, toxic amounts of 6-MP's nucleotides build up.
cards.quote: TPMT (thiopurine methyltransferase) inactivates 6-MP, so people with low TPMT build up toxic amounts of its nucleotides.
